s5.quote: Here is the culprit taken in the act
s5.note: Before this line the Chorus have chanted eight lines of marching anapaests as she is led in (ll. 376–383, printed at the end of [[s4]]). They call the sight a δαιμόνιον τέρας (_daimonion teras_, "a portent sent by a god", l. 376), which is how the ode on man looks when its abstract law-breaker turns out to be a girl they know. Their first guess at a motive is ἀφροσύνῃ (_aphrosynei_, "want of sense", l. 383), and they speak of the king's νόμοις (_nomois_, "laws", l. 382): two words she is about to take away from them. Storr's "culprit" is his own; the Guard says only "this is she, the one who did the deed" (l. 384).

s5.quote: Of giving burial. But where’s the King?
s5.note: The Greek is _tende heilomen thaptousan_ ("we caught her burying", l. 385). The verb is plain "burying", with no "attempting" about it, and the Guard repeats it at ll. 402 and 404. Creon's men never doubt that a handful of dust counts as burial. That matters for everything Creon says later about the body being unburied.

s5.quote: There from the palace he returns in time.
s5.note: The Greek is _eis deon_ ("just when needed", l. 386). Creon enters on cue here and answers with the word for coincidence, _tychei_ (l. 387). Keep the punctual entrance in mind: in the last third of the play his whole catastrophe is a matter of arriving minutes late.

s5.quote: No man, my lord, should make a vow, for if
s5.note: Like his first entrance in [[s3]], the Guard starts with a proverb before he gets to the news. Here it is that mortals should call nothing _apomoton_ ("sworn off, out of the question", l. 388). It is comic, but it is also the play's subject seen from below: here is a man for whom nothing is fixed, a few lines before a woman for whom one thing is.

s5.quote: His afterthoughts belie his first resolve.
s5.note: Literally "second thought makes a liar of judgement", with _gnomen_ (l. 389) for the judgement. The Guard means his own oath never to come back. But this is a fair summary of what happens to Creon, whose second thought arrives after Tiresias has left and is correct and useless.

s5.quote: When from the hail-storm of thy threats I fled
s5.note: The Greek is _echeimasthen_ ("I was storm-tossed", l. 391). In his first speech Creon was the helmsman keeping the ship of state upright. To the man actually on deck he is the weather. The storm word also prepares the real storm in the Guard's narrative.

s5.quote: But the wild rapture of a glad surprise
s5.note: The Greek is cooler than Storr: joy that comes _par' elpidas_ ("beyond one's hopes", l. 392) is bigger than any other pleasure. Nobody is "intoxicated". Note what the joy is about: another person's capture. The Guard is likeable and I think Sophocles means him to be, and this is still what he is pleased by.

s5.quote: Decking the grave. No lottery this time;
s5.note: The participle _kosmousa_ ("putting in order, adorning", l. 396) is the proper word for dressing the dead, and the Guard gives it to her without irony, along with the word "grave" for what is a body under dust. The lottery is the one in [[s3]], where the watch drew lots for who should carry bad news. This time he volunteered.

s5.quote: This prize is mine by right of treasure-trove.
s5.note: θοὔρμαιον (_to hermaion_, l. 397) is a windfall, a lucky find, the sort of thing Hermes drops in your path. Creon accused this man of working for pay. Here is the only profit he makes in the play, and it is her.

s5.quote: So take her, judge her, rack her, if thou wilt.
s5.note: Storr's "rack" brings in the torture chamber. The Greek pair is forensic: _krine_ ("judge", l. 399) and a verb meaning to question and refute. The Guard expects a hearing. He is right that there will be one and wrong about who will be examined in it.

s5.quote: Hence to depart well quit of all these ills.
s5.note: The word Storr spreads into "well quit" is _eleutheros_ ("free", l. 399), and Creon grants it in the same word at l. 445. Watch the free/slave vocabulary from here: Creon calls Antigone a slave at l. 479 and she answers with the same word at l. 517. The only person who leaves this scene free is the one who looked after himself.

s5.quote: Burying the man. There’s nothing more to tell.
s5.note: αὕτη τὸν ἄνδρʼ ἔθαπτε (_haute ton andr' ethapte_, l. 402): "this woman was burying the man". Four words, a feminine pronoun at one end and the male noun in the middle. In [[s3]] Creon asked "what man dared this?" and built a theory of bribed male conspirators. The grammar corrects him before anyone argues with him.

s5.quote: Hast thou thy wits? Or know’st thou what thou say’st?
s5.note: Creon cannot take it in, and the question shows why his earlier certainty was worthless. He had a complete account of the crime, with motive and paymasters, and none of it was true. He will do the same with Ismene in a hundred lines.

s5.quote: Driven from thy presence by those awful threats,
s5.note: τὰ δείνʼ ἐκεῖνʼ (_ta dein' ekein'_, "those terrible things", l. 408). This is the adjective of the ode just sung, where many things are _deina_ and nothing more so than man. The Guard uses it of Creon's threats without a thought. The word has gone from the cosmic to the petty in thirty lines.

s5.quote: Than straight we swept away all trace of dust,
s5.note: Here is the crux of the two burials. The first dusting was complete enough to alarm Creon, so why does she return? Some have argued the first was not hers at all (the Chorus in [[s3]] wondered about the gods; a few critics have proposed Ismene). I take the plain reading. She could not have known the guards would undo it, she comes back with a jug for the libations the first report never mentioned, and she finds the body stripped. Sophocles also simply needs her caught, and caught in the act.

s5.quote: And bared the clammy body. Then we sat
s5.note: "Clammy" is polite. _mydon_ (l. 410) means oozing, wet with decay, and the next line has the men sitting where the _osmen_ ("smell", l. 412) cannot reach them. The Guard is the one character who has stood near what Creon's decree actually is. When Tiresias later describes altars fouled with carrion, this is the body he means.

s5.quote: So all night long we watched, until the sun
s5.note: There is no night in the Greek, only "this went on until the sun's bright disc stood in mid-sky" (ll. 415–416). The prologue was before dawn, the first burial was found by the first day-watch, and it is now noon of the same day. Storr's extra night hides how fast the play moves: edict, crime, arrest and sentence inside a morning. Midday is also the hour at which, in Greek stories, gods tend to show themselves.

s5.quote: Smote us. A sudden whirlwind then upraised
s5.note: A _typhos_, a whirlwind (l. 418), lifts from the ground a column of dust that the Guard calls "a trouble in the sky". It fills the plain and tears the leaves from the trees. A dust-storm, in a play where dust on a corpse is the whole issue, is either weather or help. Sophocles gives no ruling.

s5.quote: And waited till the heaven-sent plague should pass.
s5.note: The Greek is _theian noson_ ("a divine sickness", l. 421). The Guard is not a theologian and may just mean "terrible", but the word is there, and the Chorus's earlier suspicion that the gods had a hand in the first burial has never been answered. Notice also _mysantes_ ("with our eyes shut"). The watchmen are not watching at the one moment that matters, and when they open their eyes she is there.

s5.quote: At last it ceased, and lo! there stood this maid.
s5.note: The Greek is _he pais horatai_ ("the child is seen", l. 423), a present passive, as if she had been produced by the storm. _Pais_ is "child" or "girl". The Chorus used it at l. 378, the Guard uses it here, and Creon will use it too. The men of the play keep her small in their nouns while she is doing the largest thing in it.

s5.quote: A piercing cry she uttered, sad and shrill,
s5.note: The verb is the one for the women's funeral shriek, and the sound is that of a _pikras ornithos_ ("a bitter bird", l. 423–424). Birds have been against Polynices so far. He came on Thebes as a screaming eagle in the entry song, and the edict leaves him for birds to eat. Now a bird is mourning him.

s5.quote: As when the mother bird beholds her nest
s5.note: The only tender image anyone gives her, and it comes from the man arresting her. It makes her a mother at the moment she gives up any chance of being one. The Greek presses this harder than Storr: the nest is called both εὐνῆς (_eunes_) and λέχος (_lechos_, l. 425), and both are ordinary words for the marriage bed, the second returning at l. 573 for her own marriage. Behind it is the Odyssey, where Odysseus and Telemachus weep more shrilly than birds whose young have been taken.

s5.quote: Robbed of its nestlings; even so the maid
s5.note: Storr's "robbed" stands for ὀρφανὸν (_orphanon_, "orphaned", l. 425). The simile says the bed is orphaned of its young, a strange use that lets the word for the bereaved child fall on a bereaved parent. Antigone is the orphan here. The image has her as mother, child and bride in two lines, which is the confusion of roles she inherits from her family.

s5.quote: And cursed the ruffians who had done this deed.
s5.note: The Greek phrase for the ruffians is "those who had done the deed" (l. 428), and it is word for word what the Guard called her at l. 384. Burial and unburial are the same "deed" in his mouth. And she curses, as her father did. The curse is aimed at the guards and lands on the man who gave the order.

s5.quote: Anon she gathered handfuls of dry dust,
s5.note: She gathers _dipsian konin_ ("thirsty dust", l. 429), carried in her bare hands. In the prologue she spoke of heaping up a tomb. What one person can do is this. It is enough ritually, and the smallness of the act against the size of the penalty is something the play wants you to feel.

s5.quote: Thrice on the dead she poured a lustral stream.
s5.note: Not lustral water. χοαῖσι τρισπόνδοισι (_choaisi trispondoisi_, l. 431) are the three drink-offerings poured to the dead, and the verb is στέφει (_stephei_, "she crowns"). She brought a bronze jug with her, so this visit was planned. Storr's "lustral" makes it a cleansing. The Greek makes it a gift, and a coronation of a body the city has declared rubbish.

s5.quote: Our quarry. Undismayed she stood, and when
s5.note: The Greek is _therometh'_ ("we hunted her down", l. 433). The ode on man praised him for netting the light-minded birds, and she has just been a bird. The praise of human skill and the arrest of Antigone use the same picture. She is "not at all frightened", which is the first thing we learn of her manner since the prologue.

s5.quote: And yet to bring disaster to a friend
s5.note: The Greek is _tous philous_ (l. 438). The Guard, a servant of the house, counts the princess among his _philoi_, his own people. So the great word of the scene is first used here, casually, by someone who then weighs it against his skin and finds it lighter. He feels both pleasure and pain and says so. Antigone does the same sum of pains at ll. 465–468 and gets the opposite answer.

s5.quote: A man’s first duty is to serve himself.
s5.note: Storr makes a maxim of it. The Guard is more personal: all this πέφυκε (_pephyke_, "is by nature", l. 440) less to me than my own σωτηρίας, safety. Hold on to the verb. At l. 523 Antigone uses the same one of herself: my nature is to join in love. Set the two natures side by side and the distance between an ordinary decent person and her is measured exactly.

s5.quote: Speak, girl, with head bent low and downcast eyes,
s5.note: This is a description in the Greek, and Storr has turned it into an order: "You there, you with your head bowed to the ground" (l. 441). She has stood silent and looking down through forty lines of the Guard's story. In a masked theatre posture is the face. I do not read it as shame, since nothing she goes on to say is ashamed. She is looking at the earth, where her business is.

s5.quote: Guilty. I did it, I deny it not.
s5.note: There is no "Guilty" in the Greek. She says "I say I did it and I do not deny it" (l. 443), affirming the act in Creon's own two verbs and pleading nothing. With that she takes the question of fact off the table. Only the question of right is left, and that is the ground she wants.

s5.quote: Now answer this plain question, yes or no,
s5.note: "Not at length, but briefly" (l. 446). She gives him one word, _eide_ ("I knew"), and then, when he asks the next question, twenty-one lines. Creon calls his edict here "what was proclaimed" (l. 447). It is still a proclamation. Watch what he calls it two lines later.

s5.quote: I knew, all knew; how should I fail to know?
s5.note: It was _emphane_ ("public, out in the open", l. 448). Is Creon offering his niece a way out through ignorance? I think he may be. If so she shuts it at once, as she told Ismene in [[s1]] she would: she wanted the deed proclaimed.

s5.quote: And yet wert bold enough to break the law?
s5.note: τούσδʼ ὑπερβαίνειν νόμους (_tousd' hyperbainein nomous_, "to overstep these laws", l. 449). The proclamation of two lines ago has become _nomoi_. And ἐτόλμας, "you dared", is the last ode's word for the daring that makes a man cityless. Creon thinks he is quoting the Chorus's verdict. Her whole reply is an attack on that one noun.

s5.quote: Yea, for these laws were not ordained of Zeus,
s5.note: Storr gives away what she refuses to concede. She does not say "laws". She says: it was not Zeus who was ὁ κηρύξας (_ho keryxas_, "the one who proclaimed", l. 450) these things to me. She keeps Creon's edict in the herald's vocabulary where it started. A proclamation needs a proclaimer with standing, and the first thing she asks is who issued this one.

s5.quote: And she who sits enthroned with gods below,
s5.note: Δίκη (_Dike_, Justice) is ξύνοικος (_xynoikos_, "sharing a house", l. 451) with the gods below. That is unusual. In Hesiod, and elsewhere in Sophocles, Justice sits beside Zeus. Antigone names Zeus for the upper world and then moves Justice downstairs to live with the dead. Her justice is the claim the dead have on the living, and she is not offering a general theory of right.

s5.quote: Justice, enacted not these human laws.
s5.note: The verb ὥρισεν (_horisen_, l. 452) is from the word for a boundary stone: Justice "marked out" no such laws among men. This is the one place she lets _nomoi_ near Creon's edict, and it is inside a negation. The manuscripts read the line differently, making it the gods who did mark out "these laws", meaning burial. On either text the point holds: the boundary was set by someone else, before Creon.

s5.quote: Nor did I deem that thou, a mortal man,
s5.note: τὰ σὰ κηρύγμαθʼ (_ta sa kerygmath'_, "your proclamations", l. 453–454), set against the _nomima_ of the gods in the next line. That contrast of nouns is the argument. θνητὸν ὄνθʼ (_thneton onth'_, "being mortal", l. 455) is left loose in the Greek and can mean "you, a mortal" or "anyone who is mortal". Storr chooses the insult. The looser sense is better: no mortal can do this, herself included.

s5.quote: Could’st by a breath annul and override
s5.note: "By a breath" is Storr's ornament. The verb is ὑπερδραμεῖν (_hyperdramein_, "to outrun", l. 455), and it answers Creon's ὑπερβαίνειν at l. 449. You say I stepped over your laws. You tried to run past the gods'. She returns his charge of transgression to him in a stronger form of his own verb.

s5.quote: The immutable unwritten laws of Heaven.
s5.note: ἄγραπτα κἀσφαλῆ θεῶν νόμιμα (_agrapta kasphale theon nomima_, l. 454–455). Not _nomoi_ but νόμιμα, "usages, things held lawful", the word for observances. And _asphale_ is "unfailing, not to be tripped up", which is firmer and more physical than "immutable". This phrase made the play a founding text for every later argument about higher law, so notice how specific she is: these are the rites owed to the dead. She claims no general licence for conscience. An Athenian audience was proud of written law, and Pericles in Thucydides also speaks of unwritten laws whose breach brings agreed disgrace.

s5.quote: They were not born today nor yesterday;
s5.note: The edict is a few hours old. She heard of it before dawn in the prologue as something just announced. Against that she sets _aei pote_ ("always, at all times", l. 456). The contrast is of age, and in Greek thinking about custom age is authority.

s5.quote: They die not; and none knoweth whence they sprang.
s5.note: The Greek is positive: ζῇ ταῦτα (_zei tauta_, "these things live", l. 457). And κοὐδεὶς οἶδεν, "no one knows", from when they appeared. She claims no revelation and names no lawgiver. That is a strength, since she cannot be asked for her source, and a limit, since she cannot produce one. The same "who knows?" comes back at l. 521 as her last argument.

s5.quote: I was not like, who feared no mortal’s frown,
s5.note: ἀνδρὸς οὐδενὸς φρόνημα δείσασʼ (_andros oudenos phronema deisas'_, "fearing no man's will", l. 458–459). The word is ἀνδρὸς, a male's, so gender enters the scene from her side first. And φρόνημα is the ode's word for the wind-swift thought man taught himself, here meaning mere temper. Creon picks the word up at l. 473 and throws it back.

s5.quote: The wrath of Heaven. I knew that I must die,
s5.note: What she says is "to pay the penalty among the gods" (ll. 459–460). So her first stated motive is not love. It is fear of a higher court, and she has compared two penalties and chosen the lighter. A tutor would ask whether that makes her prudent rather than heroic. I think it shows she reasons more coldly than her admirers allow.

s5.quote: Is thereby hastened, I shall count it gain.
s5.note: The Greek is _kerdos_ ("profit", l. 462). In [[s3]] this was Creon's word for what corrupts men: money, bribes, the hope of gain that has destroyed many. He assumes everyone has a price. She now names hers, and it is an early death. The word does not fit his meaning any more.

s5.quote: For death is gain to him whose life, like mine,
s5.note: _Kerdos_ again (l. 464), now as a general rule for anyone who lives among many evils. This is the voice of the play's first lines, where she counted over the family's sufferings. It weakens her case a little: if death is a profit, what is she giving up? She answers that herself in the Kommos ([[s9]]), where the losses are finally counted and this armour comes off.

s5.quote: To leave my mother’s son unburied there,
s5.note: τὸν ἐξ ἐμῆς μητρὸς (_ton ex emes metros_, "the one from my own mother", l. 466–467). Kinship for her is measured through the womb, as it will be again at l. 511. With it comes ἄθαπτον (_athapton_, "unburied"), the condition the whole play is about. She does not say "a human being" or "a Theban". Remember this when the speech is read as a charter of universal rights.

s5.quote: Methinks the judge of folly’s not acquit.
s5.note: The word "fool" comes three times in two lines: μῶρα, μώρῳ, μωρίαν (ll. 469–470), ending on ὀφλισκάνω (_ophliskano_), a law-court verb for losing a suit. "I am convicted of folly in a fool's court." After twenty lines on Zeus and Justice she closes with an insult. It is magnificent and it is also the moment she makes it impossible for Creon to give way without being seen to lose.

s5.quote: A stubborn daughter of a stubborn sire,
s5.note: Storr's "stubborn" tames ὠμὸν ἐξ ὠμοῦ πατρὸς (_omon ex omou patros_, l. 471). _Omos_ is "raw", the word for uncooked meat and for savagery. The elders hear the unwritten laws and their comment is on her breeding, her γέννημʼ (_gennema_). Filing her under Oedipus spares them an opinion on her argument.

s5.quote: This ill-starred maiden kicks against the pricks.
s5.note: Storr borrows from the King James Bible, where an ox kicks the goad and hurts only itself. The Greek has no ox: "she does not know how to εἴκειν (_eikein_, "yield") to troubles" (l. 472). That verb belongs to the whole play. Haemon in [[s7]] tells his father about trees that bend in the flood and live, and in the end it is Creon who has to yield. Here the Chorus fasten on her the fault that will turn out to be his.

s5.quote: Well, let her know the stubbornest of wills
s5.note: He says _skler' agan phronemata_ ("over-hard spirits", l. 473), taking her word from l. 459, and he says it to the Chorus. He will not address her directly for another twenty lines. The iron that shatters and the horse broken with a small bit are both from the ode's list of human mastery. Every image fits Creon better than her, and his son will tell him so with trees and ships.

s5.quote: Who in subjection lives must needs be meek.
s5.note: "In subjection" softens δοῦλός (_doulos_, "slave", l. 479): there is no room to think big for one who is the slave of those around him. He is speaking of his sister's daughter, a king's child. This is how Creon sees rule: one master and a household of slaves. She gives him the word back at l. 517.

s5.quote: First overstepped the established law, and then—
s5.note: νόμους ὑπερβαίνουσα τοὺς προκειμένους (_nomous hyperbainousa tous prokeimenous_, "overstepping the laws laid down", l. 481). He repeats his own phrase from l. 449 as if she had not spoken. This is the thing to notice about the central scene: Creon never answers her on Zeus or Justice, here or later. He charges her with ὕβρις (_hybris_, l. 482) twice over, which in Athenian usage is outrage that shames its victim. He is the one who feels shamed.

s5.quote: She boasts and glories in her wickedness.
s5.note: The second outrage is γελᾶν (_gelan_, "to laugh", l. 483). Being laughed at is what a Sophoclean hero cannot stand. It drives Ajax to kill himself. Antigone has not laughed. Creon hears laughter because he is afraid of it, and at l. 551 she will use the verb herself, of Ismene, with pain.

s5.quote: Unpunished, I am woman, she the man.
s5.note: There is no "woman" in the line. He says ἐγὼ μὲν οὐκ ἀνήρ, αὕτη δʼ ἀνήρ (_ego men ouk aner, haute d' aner_, l. 484): then I am no man, and she is the man, if this κράτη (_krate_, "mastery", l. 485) rests with her unpunished. This is the first time Creon says what is at stake for him. It was not in his opening speech about the ship of state. From here he says it in nearly every scene.

s5.quote: But though she be my sister’s child or nearer
s5.note: ὁμαιμονεστέρα (_homaimonestera_, "closer in blood", l. 486) than all of Ζηνὸς ἑρκείου, Zeus of the Courtyard, the god at the household altar who stands for the family itself. Storr's "all who worship at my hearth" loses the god. Creon names the divine guardian of kinship in order to say that kinship will count for nothing. And he condemns Ismene in the same breath on no evidence at all.

s5.quote: Within the palace, frenzied and distraught.
s5.note: He calls her _lyssosan_ ("raving", l. 492), and not in possession of her wits. He saw a girl beside herself and concluded guilt. It is his habit: bribery behind the first burial, conspiracy behind this one. Ismene was distraught because she knew what her sister had gone to do.

s5.quote: When caught, to make a virtue of a crime.
s5.note: καλλύνειν (_kallynein_, "to make beautiful", l. 496). Creon cannot know it, but he has hit her exact word. In [[s1]] she told Ismene it would be _kalon_, beautiful, to die doing this. He begins the sentence with μισῶ (_miso_, "I hate", l. 495). Count the verbs of hating in his part of this scene and then read l. 523 again.

s5.quote: Would’st thou do more than slay thy prisoner?
s5.note: Her first words since the insult, and they ask for the sentence. _helon_ ("having caught", l. 497) keeps the Guard's hunting language. The dry answer to her question is yes. He will think of something beyond killing her, a walled cave with a ration of food. And he has already done more than kill her brother.

s5.quote: Not I, thy life is mine, and that’s enough.
s5.note: The Greek is _tout' echon hapant' echo_ ("having this I have everything", l. 498). Storr gives the sense but not the boast. It is the sentence of a man who thinks killing her settles things. By the end of the day he has that and nothing else.

s5.quote: A name so glorious as by burying
s5.note: The Greek is _kleos eukleesteron_ (l. 502), literally "a more glorious glory". _Kleos_ is what Homeric warriors die for. So there is a third motive beside fear of the gods and love of kin: she wants fame, and says so. I do not think that discredits her. It does mean the Hegelian picture of her as pure family piety leaves out how much of the male heroic code she has taken over.

s5.quote: A brother? so my townsmen all would say,
s5.note: The brother is τὸν αὐτάδελφον (_ton autadelphon_, "my very own brother", l. 503), the word of the play's first line, where it was Ismene. And "townsmen" is too wide. She says τούτοις πᾶσιν (_toutois pasin_, "all these men here", l. 504) and means the fifteen elders standing in the orchestra. She appeals to them directly, to their faces. They do not answer.

s5.quote: A king’s prerogatives, and not the least
s5.note: Storr's "king" is _he tyrannis_ (l. 506). The word can be neutral in tragedy, but she defines it as the power to do and say what it likes, which is the Athenian democrat's definition of tyranny: rule that answers to no one. And she says it "is blessed", in a word the next ode opens with in earnest (l. 583).

s5.quote: These think as I, but bate their breath to thee.
s5.note: ὑπίλλουσιν στόμα (_hypillousin stoma_, l. 509): they curl their mouths under, as a dog tucks its tail. Creon has just said she alone of the Thebans sees it this way. Who is right about the city? Haemon will report in [[s7]] that the town mourns her in whispers. The proof on stage now is the Chorus's silence under a direct appeal.

s5.quote: To reverence kith and kin can bring no shame.
s5.note: "Kith and kin" is far too mild for τοὺς ὁμοσπλάγχνους (_tous homosplanchnous_, l. 511): those of the same _splanchna_, the same womb, the same inward parts. The verb is σέβειν (_sebein_, "to revere"), the root of the play's word for piety. She puts religious reverence and bodily kinship in one phrase. For her they are one thing.

s5.quote: One mother bare them and the self-same sire.
s5.note: Creon has made his best point: Eteocles was _homaimos_ ("of the same blood", l. 512) too. She grants it in full and adds "from one mother and the same father" (l. 513). In this family the phrase is loaded, since the same father is also their mother's son. She does not flinch from it. Sameness of blood is her whole argument.

s5.quote: Why cast a slur on one by honoring one?
s5.note: Creon now takes the piety words for his side. Her favour to Polynices is _dyssebe_ ("impious", l. 514) in Eteocles' eyes, and at l. 516 Polynices is simply "the impious one". So both of them claim _eusebeia_, and the play will not say who holds it until Tiresias does. Creon's premise is that honour is a fixed sum, so that giving some to one brother takes it from the other. She replies that the dead man will not testify to that, which she cannot know.

s5.quote: The slain man was no villain but a brother.
s5.note: οὐ γάρ τι δοῦλος, ἀλλʼ ἀδελφὸς ὤλετο (_ou gar ti doulos, all' adelphos oleto_, l. 517): it was no slave who died, but a brother. I suspect Storr's "villain" keeps its old sense of serf, but a modern reader hears "wicked man" and loses the point. She is answering Creon's "slave" of l. 479. And she shows the edge of her principle: it is for a brother. She does not say what a slave's body would be owed.

s5.quote: The patriot perished by the outlaw’s brand.
s5.note: The Greek puts each brother in half a line: one _porthon de tende gen_ ("ravaging this land", l. 518), the other standing up for it. This is Creon's real case and she never denies the fact. Athenians would have felt its force, since their own practice refused a traitor burial in Attic soil. Creon goes further than that practice did: he forbids burial anywhere and leaves the body exposed.

s5.quote: Nathless the realms below these rites require.
s5.note: Here she does say "laws": ὅ γʼ Ἅιδης τοὺς νόμους τούτους ποθεῖ (_ho g' Haides tous nomous toutous pothei_, l. 519). The noun she kept from Creon's edict she gives to burial, and makes Hades the party interested. The verb ποθεῖ is "longs for", a word for missing someone absent. Storr's "require" is too official. Her god of the dead wants these rites the way the bereaved want the dead.

s5.quote: Who knows if this world’s crimes are virtues there?
s5.note: Storr inflates it. She says τίς οἶδεν (_tis oiden_, "who knows", l. 521) whether these things are εὐαγῆ (_euage_, "free of pollution, holy") below. "These things" may be her act, or it may be Creon's distinction between the good brother and the bad. It is her best argument and her most modest. She does not claim to know the mind of the dead. She says he does not either, and that he is punishing on the assumption that he does.

s5.quote: Not even death can make a foe a friend.
s5.note: οὑχθρός and φίλος (_ho echthros_, _philos_, l. 522): the two poles of the play in one line. For Creon these are positions a man earns. In his first speech in [[s3]] he said he would never count an enemy of the city as a _philos_. For Antigone _philos_ is a fact of birth that conduct cannot cancel. They are using one word for two different things, and neither notices.

s5.quote: My nature is for mutual love, not hate.
s5.note: οὔτοι συνέχθειν, ἀλλὰ συμφιλεῖν ἔφυν (_outoi synechthein, alla symphilein ephyn_, l. 523). Both verbs appear to be coined for this line: I was born to join in loving, not to join in hating. The prefix matters. She is refusing to take a side in her brothers' enmity and choosing to share in the _philia_ she owes both. And ἔφυν, "I was born", makes it a matter of birth and so of family. It is the line everyone remembers, but she is not announcing love for mankind. She has shown Creon none, and within a minute she is refusing her sister.

s5.quote: No woman shall be the master while I live.
s5.note: He hears her verb and sneers with it three times: go below and φίλει, love them, if love you must (l. 524). Then he says ἐμοῦ δὲ ζῶντος οὐκ ἄρξει γυνή (_emou de zontos ouk arxei gyne_, l. 525), with γυνή, "woman", as the last word of the exchange. He has lost the stichomythia on every point of kinship and piety. He ends it on force and sex, with no civic argument left.

s5.quote: Weeping o’er her sister’s fate,
s5.note: Anapaests again, as for Antigone's entrance, though Storr turns them into a rhymed jingle. Ismene's tears are _philadelpha_ ("sister-loving", l. 527), a _phil_- word given to her three lines after Antigone's great one. Her face is _haimatoen_ ("blood-red", l. 528) with weeping. Storr's "angry" is his invention. The Chorus describe a face because the mask cannot show one.

s5.quote: Two plagues I nurtured blindly, so it proved,
s5.note: δύʼ ἄτα (_dy' ata_, l. 533), a dual: "a pair of ruins", with "uprisings against my throne" added. _Ate_ is the ruin the gods send through a man's own blinded judgement, and the ode that follows this scene ([[s6]]) is about nothing else. Creon uses it as abuse for two girls. He says οὐδʼ ἐμάνθανον, "I did not notice", and his failure to learn in time is the plot. Two unarmed nieces have become a coup, and one of them a viper.

s5.quote: I did the deed, if she will have it so,
s5.note: She says _dedraka tourgon_ ("I did the deed", l. 536), on the condition that her sister _homorrothei_, "rows in time with me". It is a lie, a loving one, and it comes with a glance sideways for permission. Is this the timid Ismene of the prologue? She told Antigone then that she could not act against the city. She can, it turns out, die for her sister. Those are different things, and Sophocles gives her full credit for the second.

s5.quote: That were unjust. Thou would’st not act with me
s5.note: Justice, _he dike_ (l. 538), will not allow it. This is the Justice of l. 451, now turned on Ismene. Antigone is exact about the record: you were not willing, and I did not make you a partner. Both halves are true to [[s1]], where she said she would not accept the help even if it were offered later. She forgets nothing.

s5.quote: But now thy bark is stranded, I am bold
s5.note: She calls herself _xymploun_ ("fellow-voyager", l. 541) in suffering, after the rowing verb of l. 536. Ismene thinks in ships. Creon's ship in [[s3]] was the city, on which alone one can make friends. Hers has two people in it. Storr's "stranded" is his addition, and "I am bold" underplays the Greek, "I am not ashamed".

s5.quote: A friend in word is never friend of mine.
s5.note: λόγοις δʼ ἐγὼ φιλοῦσαν οὐ στέργω φίλην (_logois d' ego philousan ou stergo philen_, l. 543). Three words of loving in one line, used to refuse love, twenty lines after "my nature is to join in love". The test is deed against word, τοὔργον against λόγοις. Is she being cruel, or keeping Ismene out of the grave? I think both. She needs the deed to be hers alone, and refusing Ismene also saves Ismene's life.

s5.quote: One death sufficeth. Wherefore should’st thou die?
s5.note: The question is Storr's. She says _arkeso thneskous' ego_ ("my dying will be enough", l. 547). Before it comes a prohibition: do not make your own what you never touched. Burial is done with the hands, and Ismene's were not there. In the same line she says "do not die with me", using _koina_ ("in common"), the word with which she first greeted Ismene.

s5.quote: What would life profit me bereft of thee?
s5.note: No "profit" here. Storr has borrowed the scene's other key word by mistake. Ismene asks what _bios_ ("life") is _philos_ ("dear") to her without her sister (l. 548). She is speaking Antigone's language of _philia_ back to her, and it is refused.

s5.quote: Ask Creon, he’s thy kinsman and best friend.
s5.note: One word does the work of Storr's two: κηδεμών (_kedemon_, l. 549), the one who has you in his care, a guardian. Its root covers family care, connexion by marriage and the tending of the dead, which is everything Antigone thinks Creon has betrayed. It is the cruellest line she speaks, and it throws the prologue back at a sister who has come to die with her.

s5.quote: ’Tis a sad mockery, if indeed I mock.
s5.note: The participle _algousa_ ("in pain", l. 551) is the first word: it is in pain that I laugh at you, if I do laugh. This is the one crack in her manner in the whole scene. Creon accused her of laughing over her deed (l. 483). She admits to this laughter, and to what it costs her.

s5.quote: No, save thyself; I grudge not thy escape.
s5.note: The Greek is _soson seauten_ (l. 553). It is the Guard's creed, safety first, recommended to Ismene. Does she mean it kindly? This is the strongest line for the protective reading, and I think the tone has changed since l. 549. She will not share the deed, but she does want her sister alive.

s5.quote: Well, some approved thy wisdom, others mine.
s5.note: Storr loses who the "some" and "others" are. The verb is _phronein_ ("to think rightly", l. 557). The usual reading, which I accept, is that Ismene seemed wise to those up here and Antigone to those below. Good sense has two juries in this play, the living and the dead. The Chorus's last lines award the prize for it, too late.

s5.quote: Fear not; thou livest, I died long ago
s5.note: The Greek is _he d' eme psyche palai tethneken_ (l. 559–560): my soul has long been dead. Since when? Since the decision before the play began, or since the family's ruin that she counted over in its first lines. The end of the sentence is "so as to help the dead", which Storr turns into a heroic "gave my life". She speaks as someone already below. Creon's sentence, a living woman shut in a tomb, will make her claim literal.

s5.quote: Both maids, methinks, are crazed. One suddenly
s5.note: Creon has stood silent for twenty-five lines while the sisters talk past him. His word is _anoun_ ("mindless", l. 562), and it is the word Ismene used of Antigone at the end of [[s1]]. One of them, he says, has been so from birth. He has heard the scene's two great speeches and put both down to a defect of mind.

s5.quote: thy sister’s dead.
s5.note: Ismene has said "without her", using the pronoun for someone present, ἥδε (_hede_, "this woman here"). Creon forbids it: do not say ἥδε, for she no longer exists (l. 567). She is standing a few feet away. Antigone said the same of herself a moment ago, so on this one point they agree.

s5.quote: What, wilt thou slay thy own son’s plighted bride?
s5.note: Line 568, nearly halfway through the play, and this is the first we hear that Antigone is betrothed to Creon's son. Ismene says it. Antigone did not mention him in the prologue or in her defence, and Creon has not thought of him. Sophocles held the fact back so that it falls here, after the sentence. We now know the edict will reach into Creon's own house.

s5.quote: Aye, let him raise him seed from other fields.
s5.note: Storr's biblical "raise seed" dignifies a barnyard line: ἀρώσιμοι γὰρ χἀτέρων εἰσὶν γύαι (_arosimoi gar chateron eisin gyai_, "others have furrows that can be ploughed", l. 569). The Athenian betrothal formula gave a daughter "for the ploughing of legitimate children", so the metaphor is conventional and he makes it brutal. The ode praised man for wearing down the Earth with the plough. For Creon a wife is a field, and one field is as good as another.

s5.quote: No new espousal can be like the old.
s5.note: The Greek is _hermosmena_ ("fitted together", l. 570): not as things were fitted between him and her. This is all the testimony the play gives that the match was more than an arrangement, and it comes from Ismene. Antigone says nothing. Haemon, when he comes, will argue politics and never plead love.

s5.quote: A plague on trulls who court and woo our sons.
s5.note: Storr's "trulls who court and woo" is his own invention. The line is κακὰς ἐγὼ γυναῖκας υἱέσι στυγῶ (_kakas ego gynaikas hyiesi stygo_, "I hate bad wives for my sons", l. 571). The verb is one of loathing, the second such verb Creon has used since l. 495. Against her "I was born to join in love" he has now said "I hate" twice in so many words.

s5.quote: O Haemon, how thy sire dishonors thee!
s5.note: Storr drops the most important word: ὦ φίλταθʼ Αἷμον (_o philtath' Haimon_, "dearest Haemon", l. 572), the superlative of _philos_. The manuscripts give the line to Ismene. A Renaissance edition moved it to Antigone, and Jebb and Storr follow, because it seems too warm to leave her silent. I can believe it either way but I lean to Ismene: the exchange around it is hers and Creon's line for line, and Antigone's silence about Haemon then runs unbroken to her death. If the line is hers, it is the only time she names him.

s5.quote: A plague on thee and thy accursed bride!
s5.note: No curse in the Greek: "you vex me too much, you and _to son lechos_", l. 573. The phrase means "your marriage-bed" if Antigone has just spoken, or "this marriage you keep on about" if Ismene has, so it settles nothing about the speaker. _Lechos_ is the word the Guard used for the bird's emptied nest at l. 425.

s5.quote: ’Tis death that bars this marriage, not his sire.
s5.note: Ἅιδης ὁ παύσων τούσδε τοὺς γάμους ἔφυ (_Haides ho pauson tousde tous gamous ephy_, l. 575): Hades is the one who will stop this marriage. "Not his sire" is Storr's addition, though it is the evasion Creon intends. Read the line again after the Messenger's speech, where Haemon lies with his arms round her in the tomb and gets his wedding in the house of Hades. Hades does not stop the marriage. He hosts it.

s5.quote: By you, as first by me; off with them, guards,
s5.note: The Chorus have said _dedogmen'_ ("it is resolved", l. 576), the verb of formal decrees. Creon's reply is "yes, by you and by me" (l. 577). He writes the elders into the sentence and they let him. Their one protest in the scene was about the son's marriage, not the niece's life or the corpse. Antigone said fear had locked their tongues. This is what that looks like.

s5.quote: To live as women use, not roam at large.
s5.note: The Greek is _gynaikas einai tasde med' aneimenas_ (l. 579): these must be women, and not let loose. The participle is used of animals turned out to range. The play began with two sisters outside the house gates before dawn, where they should not have been. Creon's last order is to put them back indoors. Ismene goes in condemned too, and is not spared until l. 771.

s5.quote: When they perceive death pressing on life’s heels.
s5.note: Even the _thraseis_ ("the bold", l. 580) run when they see Hades close. He has misjudged her to the last. She does not run. The one who gives way when death comes near his house is Creon. The Chorus begin the next ode on the word _eudaimones_ ("blessed", l. 583), which no one on stage now is.
